Replay

Adding and evolving a Replay feature

5 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Register an enemyBake a shared content catalogFreeze before changing a contractExercise the featureCosts and scopeCurrent adapter declarations

Use Scrapyard to follow the optional Replay helpers through enemy registration, content baking, schema conversion, and feature tests. Godot authors scene composition and local appearance; Odin values contain gameplay state, decisions, and configuration. Stormcaller exercises all four steps. The typed adapter layer owns binding configuration, asset lifetimes, view traversal, and contextual diagnostics.

Register an enemy#

  1. Create a MobDef under data/mobs, with a stable ID within MAX_MOBS. Add nested gameplay Resources such as PulseDef there; the shared extractor checks ranges and copies their values. Implement new behavior in the pure reducer.
  2. Create a style under visuals/enemies and compose a scene implementing ScrapEnemyView. Edit child geometry, animation and effects normally in Godot.
  3. Add a ScrapEnemyArchetype Resource under archetypes/enemies, referencing that definition, scene and style. The definition supplies its gameplay ID.
  4. Preview the scene with its single exported appearance, then exercise real gameplay in the workbench. No new enemy-view field or skin-array mapping is needed.

The loader checks every catalog ID has a registration, rejects duplicates and invalid scene/style references, and retains the assets for the view owner's lifetime. The adapter selects by copied display ID; the view remains concerned with one enemy. New IDs still require deliberate gameplay/version decisions. Framework API and bounds.

Bake a shared content catalog#

Baking validates authored Godot Resources and copies their gameplay values into a portable catalog. Tests and headless servers can load that catalog without opening the editor.

Interactive content_load and dev/export_content.tscn call the same scripts/content.odin extractor. After building/importing the current project:

Shell
GODOT=/path/to/godot python3 examples/replay_scrapyard/tools/stock.py \
  --project /absolute/path/to/built/project
python3 examples/replay_scrapyard/tools/stock.py --check

Check in shared/content/stock.rpldef and stock.manifest.json together. Headless servers/tests decode this artifact; there is no second gameplay-value parser. Godot remains required to rebake authored Resources, while --check only needs Python. The manifest covers nested data Resources, definition scripts, the extractor/exporter and catalog declarations. Cosmetic scenes/styles do not change this gameplay artifact.

The command compares project sources, checks generated binding guards, and requires the running compiled exporter/catalog hashes to match. Resource-only edits can be rebaked directly; extractor/type edits need a rebuilt library. Export goes to a temporary file and must pass before replacing either committed file. An interruption between the two replacements leaves a pair that --check rejects. Invalid content never replaces the last valid pair. Source hashes/checksums are build consistency checks, not a trust or authentication mechanism.

World receives a copied catalog. Editing a Resource after admission cannot alter live gameplay. The host's catalog still travels in snapshots/checkpoints. Reopening a run admits a new value; changing schemas or rules still needs version policy.

Freeze before changing a contract#

replay/evolution.freeze creates self-contained old value declarations; contract creates a reviewable canonical manifest. scaffold lists additive fields and refuses to convert until their defaults are explicitly reviewed. Changed/removed fields require authored mapping code. The tools do not infer historical reducer compatibility.

Scrapyard's actual old codec uses shared/revisions/content49/catalog.odin, with no live type dependencies. The content49→50 converter explicitly supplies zero pulse defaults and copies all prior canonical leaf bytes. Tests verify each prior leaf, assert the zero defaults and decode a real old checkpoint. Use tools/revision to produce a separate review directory; keep old reducers and fixtures with their declared contracts. API and limits.

Exercise the feature#

Use replay/testing.correction to compare predicted input followed by late correction against an uninterrupted reference, including events. Use takeover to roundtrip a checkpoint, change authority epoch, continue, audit and compare. Assert feature-specific state in the returned before/after frames.

Stormcaller tests remaining charge time, one hit, a late escape, death interruption and old-save conversion. Its native/WASM corpus uses the same takeover helper. The peer runner supplies bounded process/log ownership while the game's real-peer script checks warnings, damage/dodge and convergence under configured latency. Harness contracts.

Shell
REPLAY_AUTHORING_OUT=/absolute/fresh/results \
  nix develop --command bash tests/replay_authoring/run.sh

This runs focused definition/schema/evolution/scenario checks, native/WASM feature comparison, authored scenes/negative registrations, canonical export rejection and real peers. It is not a full parity campaign across every game.

Costs and scope#

Measured native optimized stock loading is about 1.7 ms per call on the development machine, versus roughly 0.25 µs for the old literal table. It compiles a schema and validates/decodes on each cold load: about 449 KiB peak tracked allocation and 1.04 MiB cumulative allocation, with zero retained allocations. Avoid stock() in tick/frame loops. Long-lived content users can keep their own compiled Store/schema.

The scene pool uses 257,152 bytes of Odin buffer payload versus 24,576 for the previous single-scene pool at capacity 64, ID limit 8 and seven registrations: 232,576 bytes extra (about 227 KiB), excluding allocator overhead and Godot assets. It also partitions display items by kind each presentation. We have not established a frame-time improvement. Its purpose is authored variation and reliable ownership; the single-scene and specialized rendering APIs remain available.

The takeover corpus still hashes to 8825198089392801664 on native and executed WASM. Its peak is 88,527,978 tracked bytes and cumulative allocation 197,797,441, with zero live allocations at completion. Allocation totals include testing and cold loading; they are not steady-state simulation costs.

Exact receipts and limits. Kit, the sibling original game, gameplay rules and network/content versions are unchanged by these tools.

Current adapter declarations#

The enemy script declares its display field and typed hooks once:

Odin
//gd:replay_view value=value,present=enemy_view_present,validate=enemy_view_validate,retired=enemy_view_retire,appearance=skin,configure=enemy_view_configure

Scriptgen produces scrap_enemy_view_replay_binding(). The game initializes Script_Archetypes with that descriptor, a catalog and an explicit kind selector. The owner retains the required assets and callback configuration; the candidate registry can close immediately. Presentation and notice traversal need no raw callback casts or access to pool/index internals.

The player-character view uses the simpler declaration without appearance/configure:

Odin
//gd:replay_view value=value,present=runner_view_present,validate=runner_view_validate

Its generated Script_View descriptor binds four permanent player-character scenes. Scrapyard calls these characters runners. Body generations, warps, and epochs reset cues inside each runner script; they do not respawn its node. Enemy view scope explicitly includes run/floor and observed rewind policy through Scope_Tracker. Sampling and feedback policies remain visible game code.

Both views use typed onready component fields. Enemy F6 scenes supply a ScrapEnemyPreview Resource that references a definition and sample attack state; there is no preview-kind switch. The sample is baked at scene startup using the same defs.bake_mob function as gameplay/export. Use the isolated preview refresh controls to load saved gameplay values into the isolated preview; see the editor workflow. Generic Resource batches and checked access/narrowing helpers support the explicit mapping. Codegen neither infers it from Inspector hints nor generates a second extractor.

Adapter acceptance records codegen regression, component/ownership checks, independent ID-7 preview, native/WASM equality, real revive peers and host-crash takeover.

The Replay editor dock and ability workbench now expose validation, baking, current/stale status, Resource references, draft scaffolding, reproduction verification and scenario jobs through Godot.
